lede: Many questions are about existence: which accounts have been used, which have never been used, which transactions point at nothing. A semi join keeps the rows that have a match and an anti join keeps the rows that don't, without adding a single column or duplicating a row.
objectives: Keep the rows that have at least one match with a `left_semi` join
Keep the rows that have no match with a `left_anti` join
Explain why an inner join can repeat rows where a semi join can't
Find orphan rows, including rows whose key is NULL

blocks.md:
`accounts` has one row per bank account and `transactions` one row per payment, each with an `account_id`. Suppose you want the accounts that have been used. An inner join finds them, but it gives one row per **transaction**, and it brings every transaction column along.

`how="left_semi"` asks a simpler question: does this left row have at least one match? If yes, the row is kept once, exactly as it was.

blocks.title: Semi join: each matching row once
blocks.code:
inner = accounts.join(transactions, on="account_id", how="inner")
semi = accounts.join(transactions, on="account_id", how="left_semi")

print(accounts.count(), "accounts,", inner.count(), "rows after an inner join,", semi.count(), "after a semi join")
semi.orderBy("account_id").show()
blocks.note: Three accounts have transactions. The inner join repeats them once per transaction, 12 rows in all; the semi join keeps each once, with only the account columns.

blocks.md: `how="left_anti"` is the opposite: keep the left rows that have **no** match on the right. It answers "which accounts were never used?" directly, without joining and then hunting for NULLs.

blocks.title: Anti join: rows with no match
blocks.note: Five accounts have never had a transaction. Semi plus anti always gives back every left row: 3 + 5 = 8.

blocks.md: Turn the question around and the anti join becomes a data-quality check. Transactions whose `account_id` isn't in `accounts` are **orphans**: they point at nothing. A NULL key never matches anything, not even another NULL, so a transaction with no account is always an orphan too.

blocks.title: Orphan transactions
blocks.note: T000013 names an account the bank doesn't have, and T000002 lost its account on the way in. Both need attention before anyone totals the feed by account.

blocks.md: The right side can be any DataFrame, including a filtered one. To find accounts with a particular kind of activity, filter the transactions first, then semi join.

blocks.title: Match against a filtered table
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

online = transactions.filter(F.col("channel") == "online")

accounts.join(online, on="account_id", how="left_semi").select("account_id", "customer_id", "account_type").orderBy("account_id").show()
blocks.note: Two transactions were online, but one has no account, so only A00006 is kept.

blocks.title: The right side's columns aren't there
blocks.note: A semi join only filters the left side, so `amount` doesn't exist in the result. If you need columns from the right, you need an ordinary join and must think about repeated rows.

concept.prompt: An account has 4 transactions. How many times does it appear in `accounts.join(transactions, on="account_id", how="left_semi")`?
concept.why: A semi join keeps a left row once if it has at least one match, however many matches there are.

concept.prompt: A transaction's `account_id` is NULL. Is it in `transactions.join(accounts, on="account_id", how="left_anti")`?
choices: No, NULL rows are always dropped by joins
Only if accounts also has a NULL account_id
Yes, because a NULL key never matches anything
concept.why: NULL is never equal to anything, so the row has no match and the anti join keeps it.

concept.prompt: Which columns does `accounts.join(transactions, on="account_id", how="left_anti")` have?
concept.why: Semi and anti joins filter the left side; they never add the right side's columns.

review: `how="left_semi"` keeps each left row that has at least one match, once, with only its own columns.
`how="left_anti"` keeps each left row that has no match.
An inner join repeats a left row once per match; a semi join never does.
A NULL key never matches, so an anti join always keeps rows whose key is NULL.
Anti joins find orphans: rows that point at something that doesn't exist.
Filter the right side first to ask about a particular kind of match.
